items.can_do: Can use 'and' to join a limited range of common adjectives.
Can use 'very' with a limited range of common gradable adjectives.
Can use a limited range of adjectives attributively, before a noun. ► noun phrases
Can use a limited range of adjectives predicatively, after 'be'.
Can use the irregular superlative adjective 'best' in the phrase 'my best friend'.

items.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
items.can_do: Can use 'soon' in the phrases 'See you soon' and 'Get well soon', as a signing-off device.

items.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
items.can_do: Can use a limited range of adverbs ('here', 'there') to indicate place.

items.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
items.can_do: Can use 'really' and 'very much' with verbs expressing preference ('like', 'love'), for emphasis.

items.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
items.can_do: Can use 'very' to make adjectives stronger.

items.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
items.can_do: Can use a limited range of adverbs ('always', 'sometimes') to talk about frequency.
Can use 'very' to modify common gradable adjectives.
Can use 'very' to modify time adverbs. ► adverb phrases
Can use place adverbs ('here', 'there') as complements of verbs.

items.guideword: FORM: DEGREE and TIME, MODIFYING VERBS
items.can_do: Can use degree and time adverbs to modify verbs.
Can use a limited range of adverbs in front position.
Can use a limited range of degree adverbs before an adjective.
Can use frequency adverbs in the usual mid position, between the subject and the main verb.
Can use 'really' in the usual mid-position, between the subject and the main verb.
Can use time adverbs in the usual end position.
Can use place adverbs in the usual end position.
Can modify adverbs of time and degree with 'very'.
Can omit the subject in a second main declarative clause when the subject is obvious or the same as the first clause.
Can combine two main declarative clauses using co-ordinating conjunctions ('and', 'but', 'or').
Can form simple affirmative declarative clauses.
Can form a simple negative declarative clause with lexical 'be' + 'not' or 'n't'.
Can form simple negative declarative clauses.

items.guideword: FORM: AFFIRMATIVE DECLARATIVE, MODAL AUXILIARY VERBS
items.can_do: Can form an affirmative declarative clause with modal verbs.
Can form interrogative clauses with 'be'.
Can use a finite subordinate clause with 'because', after a main clause, to introduce reasons.
Can use single word conjunctions ('and, but, or') to combine phrases.
Can use single word conjunctions ('and, but, or') to combine sentences.
Can use 'and' and 'or' before the final item in a list.
Can use single word conjunctions ('and, but, or') to combine clauses.
Can use single word conjunctions ('and, but, or') to connect single nouns and adjectives.
Can use 'but' to add an unexpected contrast.
Can use 'because' as a subordinating conjunction to introduce a subordinate clause.
Can use articles 'the', 'a' and 'an' before nouns. ► noun phrases
Can use 'a' + 'very' + adjectives in basic noun phrases. ► adverbs ►  noun phrases
Can use 'a' and 'an' before adjectives in a noun phrase. ► adjectives ►  noun phrases
Can use 'the' in prepositional phrases relating to time.
Can use no article before a limited range of nouns in some fixed expressions with prepositions.
Can use no article before a limited range of singular, plural and uncountable nouns when referring to things in general.
Can use 'this' in a limited range of contexts to refer to places from the speaker's or writer's point of view. ► noun phrases ►  pronouns: demonstrative
Can use 'this' with time and date words to refer to 'the one that's coming'.
Can use 'this' with singular nouns. ► noun phrases ►  pronouns: demonstrative
Can use possessive determiners 'my', 'your', 'his', 'her' and 'our' before nouns. ► noun phrases ► possessive pronouns
Can use a limited range of quantifying determiners with plural nouns ('some', 'lots of', 'a lot of' and numbers).
Can use a limited range of quantifying determiners with singular nouns ('a', 'every').► determiners: articles
Can use the affirmative forms 'will' and ''ll'.
Can use 'will' and ''ll' to talk about plans and intentions.
Can use the affirmative form.
Can use the affirmative question form.
Can use the negative forms.
Can use 'can' to make an offer.
Can use 'can' to talk about ability to do something.
Can use 'can' to make a request.
Can use 'can' to talk about possibility.
Can use the affirmative forms.
Can use 'will' to talk about plans and intentions.
Can use 'would like to invite' to make invitations.
Can use the affirmative form with 'like'.
Can use 'would like' to talk about wishes and preferences.
Can form negative statements of main verbs in the present simple with 'don't' + main verb. ► present simple ► can
Can form negative statements of main verb 'be', with contracted and uncontracted forms.
Can use negative form 'can’t'.
Can form simple noun phrases by pre-modifying plural nouns with an adjective and no determiner.
Can form simple noun phrases by pre-modifying singular and plural nouns with an adjective after a determiner.
Can form simple noun phrases with a limited range of determiners + singular and plural nouns. ► Nouns and noun phrases: functions
Can form noun phrases by pre-modifying a limited range of nouns with another noun.
Can use proper nouns with a capital letter to refer to specific people, places, days and things.
Can use a limited range of common nouns.
Can use a range of compound nouns, as one-word, two-word and hyphenated compounds, formed from verb + noun, noun + noun and adjective + noun combinations.
Can form plurals by adding '-s' to common countable nouns.
Can use nouns and noun phrases as subjects of the clause.
Can use nouns and noun phrases as complements of prepositions in prepositional phrases.
Can use nouns and noun phrases as objects of the clause.
Can use nouns and noun phrases as adjuncts in some time expressions.
Can use nouns and noun phrases as complements of the verb 'be'.
Can use the affirmative form with a limited range of regular and irregular verbs.
Can use the past simple to talk about everyday events or states.
Can form prepositional phrases with a preposition and a noun phrase.
Can use a limited range of simple (single-word) prepositions.
Can use the affirmative form.
Can use the present continuous with a limited range of verbs to talk about situations and events in progress.
Can use the negative form with a limited range of regular and irregular verbs.
Can use the present simple to talk about repeated events or habits, and general facts.
Can use the affirmative form with a limited range of regular and irregular verbs.
Can use the present simple with the adverb 'really' as an intensifier. ► adverbs
Can use the pronouns 'you' and 'it' after 'be' in question forms.
Can use the pronoun 'it' as a direct object to refer to an object or situation already referred to.
Can use the object pronouns 'me', 'you', 'him', 'her', 'it', 'us' and 'them' in the object position after prepositions.
Can use the pronouns 'I', 'you', 'we' and 'they' after an auxiliary or modal verb in question forms.
Can use the pronouns 'me', 'you', 'him', 'her', 'us' and 'them' in the direct object position after a transitive verb.
Can use the pronoun 'it' before 'be' to refer to a first person speaker or writer.
Can use the pronouns 'I', 'you', 'he', 'she', 'it', 'we' and 'they' in the subject position before a verb in statements.
Can use a limited range of indefinite pronouns as objects.
Can use 'everything' as subject, with a singular verb.
Can use a limited range of modal verbs + subject + main verb to form 'yes/no' questions.  ► can
Can use a limited range of prepositional verbs followed by noun or pronoun objects.
Can use auxiliary verb 'be'. ►  present continuous
Can use a limited range of modal auxiliary verbs ('can', 'will', 'would').
Can use linking verb 'be'.
Can use regular and irregular main verbs in simple verb phrases. ► present simple ► past simple
Can use a limited range of verbs followed by a 'to'- infinitive.
Can use 'would like to' + infinitive.
Can use 'like' followed either by a 'to'-infinitive or an '-ing' form, with no change in meaning.
Can use 'there is' + singular noun phrase as complement.
Can use 'there are' + plural noun phrase as complement.
Can use linking verb 'be' with complements.

crosscheck_source: Pearson GSE Grammar for adult learners 2023
crosscheck_policy: GSE Grammar is supporting/cross-check evidence mapped to reviewed grammar supercategories; it does not create a second independent target inventory.
grammar_family_stage_policy: Only lifecycle stages explicitly present in the reviewed grammar-family source are copied; missing early-level stages are not invented.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can ask basic questions using ‘What’s your ...?’
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: What’s your name? What’s your job?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Pronoun | Question words Verb | Tags and question forms Clause | With ‘be’

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use the correct form of ‘be’ with singular and plural nouns.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: The coffee is hot. The boys are Spanish. I’m Chinese. We’re students.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Basic construction Clause | With ‘be’ Noun | Plural

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can make basic statements with subject + verb + object.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I like rock music. She drinks coffee. We study English.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use subject personal pronouns.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I, you, he, she, it, we, they

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can say their own age using ‘I’m [number]’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I’m 25. I’m fifty.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can make simple statements with ‘it’s/it is’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: It’s cold. It’s ten o’clock. It’s Monday today. It’s easy. It’s late.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Phrase | With ‘be’ Pronoun | Generic/impersonal Clause | Basic construction

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use regular nouns in the plural form.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Boys, classes, books, pens, days, chairs

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use subject pronouns with the correct form of the verb ‘be’ in the simple present.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I’m French. They’re old. She’s nice.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Pronoun | Personal Clause | With ‘be’ Clause | Basic construction

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use possessive adjectives such as ‘my’, ‘your’, etc.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: my hand, your house, his mother, her sister

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘a/an’ with the names of jobs.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I’m a teacher She’s an accountant.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can form questions with ‘what’ and ‘who’ and answer them.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: What’s this? It’s my phone. Who’s that? It’s the new teacher.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Pronoun | Question words Pronoun | Personal Verb | Tags and question forms

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can ask someone’s age using ‘How old …?’
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: How old are you? How old is Nigel?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Determiner | Quantifiers Verb | Tags and question forms Clause | With ‘be’

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘and’ to link nouns and noun phrases.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: boys and girls a cat and a dog the tall man and the short woman

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use the verb ‘be’ in the simple present with adjectives.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I’m happy. It’s cold. Her hair’s long and dark. They’re not friendly.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘this is’ for an introduction.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: This is Maria. This is my sister. This is my teacher.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Determiner | Deictic (this/that) Clause | Basic construction Phrase | With ‘be’

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use common forms of ‘have’ in the present tense.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I have a sister.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use common irregular nouns in the plural form.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: People, women, children

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can ask where other people are using ‘Where is/are …?’
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Where’s the bathroom? Where are your children?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Pronoun | Question words Verb | Tags and question forms Clause | With ‘be’

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘a/an’ with single countable nouns.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: a good film, an interesting lesson, an hour

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can make affirmative statements using the present simple without time reference.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: present simple for facts and states (affirmative only)
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: He lives in the city. She’s married. He works for Siemens.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can make negative statements using the present simple.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: He doesn’t understand. I don’t speak Japanese.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can ask wh- questions using the present simple.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: wh- questions in the present simple
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: What do you want? Where does she live?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Verb | Tags and question forms Pronoun | Question words

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use the present simple to refer to daily routines.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: He gets the bus to work. I drink six cups of tea a day.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can ask yes/no questions using the present simple.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: yes/no questions in the present simple
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Do you know her? Does he want a drink?

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘a/an’ with jobs to talk about work and professions.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: She’s a teacher. I’m a student. He’s an architect.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use basic prepositions of place with nouns and noun phrases.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: The money’s in my bag. The wine is on the dining-room table. The church is opposite my uncle’s house.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Preposition | Place Adverb | Place & movement Clause | Basic construction

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use verbs in the imperative.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Tell me! Don’t speak to me! Help me!

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use personal pronouns as objects and complements.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I like him. I can see her. He wants us.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use a range of time expressions with whole numbers (+ ‘o’clock’).
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: three o’clock nine (o’clock) in the morning

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘there’ + ‘be’ to express presence/ absence.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: There’s a small house. There isn’t a window.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can ask about the price of something using ‘How much is/are …?’
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: How much is a sandwich? How much are the tomatoes?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Determiner | Quantifiers Verb | Tags and question forms Clause | With ‘be’

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can ask a range of wh- questions.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: What’s this? Who’s that? Where’s your house?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Pronoun | Question words Clause | Basic construction Verb | Tags and question forms

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can say where they and other people are using a few basic prepositions.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: NP + ‘is/are’ + PP with common prepositions of place
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: John’s in the bar. My parents are at home.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use the present simple to refer to likes, dislikes and opinions.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: present simple for opinions, likes and dislikes
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I like football. I don’t like tennis. Do you like pop music? I think it’s delicious.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘but’ to link clauses and sentences.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: She likes coffee, but I like tea. She’s good at maths but not English.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Conjunction | Concession and contrast Clause | Comparison

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use common forms of ‘have got’ (BrE) in the present tense.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Have you got a car? (BrE)

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can give dates (e.g. their date of birth) using ordinal numbers in the form day- month-year or month-day-year.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: ordinal number + month/month + ordinal number + year
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: The thirteenth of May 1979 September the 5th 1986

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘’s’ to express possession with singular nouns.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Diego’s book my friend’s car

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can construct short answers to questions in the present simple using the verb ‘do’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: tag responses (short answers to present simple yes/no questions)
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Yes, I do. No, I don’t. Yes, they do. Yes, she does.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Verb | Tags and question forms Verb | Auxiliary

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can tell when to use the present simple and when to use the present continuous.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I get up at 7 o’clock every day. It’s 7 o’clock and I’m getting up now.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘I’d like …/I want …’ to express wants and wishes.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I’d like a drink. I want a burger.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘can’ to refer to ability in the present.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I can swim. She can’t understand that book.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use negative forms of the simple past.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: They didn’t understand. She didn’t catch her plane.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Verb | Tense Clause | Negation Verb | Negative forms
